title: Guruship to the Granth
hook: the day in 1708 the Guru Granth Sahib became Guru is marked each autumn

segments.voice: Yesterday, the first installation, and your line: the word installed. Did you give one book a place of honor? A hundred and four years after that first opening, the book received something more than a place. Day six hundred ninety-one.

A community led by a living teacher meets a hard question sooner or later: what happens after? Who guides it when the teacher is gone? For the Sikhs, that question came to a head in 1708, far from Punjab, at Nanded in the Deccan, by the Godavari river. Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Guru, had been gravely wounded. His four sons had all died before him. The Sikhs around him asked who would guide them next. Today: Gurta Gaddi.
screen: `WHAT HAPPENS AFTER?` → `NANDED, 1708.` → `WHO WILL GUIDE US NEXT?`

segments.voice: Gurta Gaddi means the throne of guruship: gaddi is the seat, the cushion of authority, and gurta is the office of the Guru. Sikh tradition remembers what happened at Nanded in 1708. Guru Gobind Singh placed five coins and a coconut before the Granth, the same sign used when one Guru installed the next, and bowed to it. He declared that after him there would be no human Guru. The Granth itself, now called the Guru Granth Sahib, would be the Guru. For Sikhs, not only a holy book, but the Guru, living in the Word. Tradition says that not long before, at Damdama Sahib, the Granth had been completed with the hymns of his father, Guru Tegh Bahadur. So the Word was whole. Sikhs also speak of the Guru Panth, the community of the Khalsa, as carrying the Guru's authority together, guided by the Granth. And after the Ardas, sangats often sing a couplet that says: by the command of the Timeless One the Panth was established; all Sikhs are commanded to accept the Granth as Guru. That couplet comes from later Sikh writings rather than the Granth itself, but it puts the teaching in a line sangats sing together. What follows is simple and large. In Sikh understanding, every Sikh, anywhere in the world, has direct access to the Guru. No human successor standing between a Sikh and the Guru. Just the Word, opened each morning, read each night. The Gurta Gaddi Divas is marked each autumn with kirtan, readings and processions, especially at Hazur Sahib in Nanded.
screen: `GURTA GADDI: THE THRONE OF GURUSHIP.` · `NANDED: FIVE COINS AND A COCONUT.` · `THE WORD, COMPLETE AT DAMDAMA.` · `THE GURU IN EVERY SIKH'S REACH.` · then, large: `THE ETERNAL GURU.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bow to the Granth. If there's a Guru Granth Sahib or a gutka near you, go to it, and bow, the way Sikhs do on entering the darbar. If there isn't, picture one: the Granth on its raised seat, covered in cloth, a granthi waving the chaur above it. Bow your head toward that picture, slowly. Let the bow mean: I'm ready to listen. If you pray, you can say Waheguru as you rise. The bell holds the time.
Gurta Gaddi. The throne of guruship, given by Guru Gobind Singh to the Granth at Nanded in 1708: from then on, Sikhs revere the Guru Granth Sahib as the Guru.
Your line: the eternal guru. Today, when you need guidance, open a page of words you trust before you open your phone. Day six hundred ninety-one.
